```{r}
#| include: false
s <- jsonlite::fromJSON("results/summary.json")
f <- function(x) sprintf("%.2f", x)
n <- function(x) format(x, big.mark = ",", scientific = FALSE, trim = TRUE)
show_code <- function(path, language, section = NULL) {
  lines <- readLines(path, warn = FALSE)
  if (!is.null(section)) {
    start <- which(lines == paste("# BEGIN", section)) + 1
    end <- which(lines == paste("# END", section)) - 1
    lines <- lines[start:end]
  }
  cat(paste0("\n```", language, "\n", paste(lines, collapse = "\n"), "\n```\n"))
}
```

Could income mobility look stronger simply because we measured people in the wrong year? A parent might receive an unusually large bonus, while their adult child is still building a career. Neither income necessarily reflects what that person usually earns. Mistaking these temporary differences for lasting ones could make economic opportunity appear more open than it is.

This has happened in real research. Using the Panel Study of Income Dynamics (PSID), [Solon (1992)](https://ideas.repec.org/a/aea/aecrev/v82y1992i3p393-408.html) showed that earlier U.S. estimates were biased downward by measurement error, unrepresentative samples, or both, implying much less mobility than they suggested. [Mazumder (2005)](https://ideas.repec.org/a/tpr/restat/v87y2005i2p235-255.html) later found that averaging fathers' earnings over only a few years still understated the elasticity by roughly 30% or more.

To see why, I use SQL inside Python to match `r n(s$children)` children from `r n(s$families)` **simulated families** to their parents. The database uses a simplified structure inspired by PSID identifiers and family relationships. Every value is simulated, so the true relationship is known.

## Match the people before comparing their incomes

The [README](https://github.com/yipin-grena/aeds6400-blog/tree/main/posts/sql-income-mobility) explains setup: `run.py` builds the data and SQLite database, and `tutorial.py` runs the comparisons below. Four tables carry the analysis.

| Table | One row represents | Important columns |
|---|---|---|
| `individuals` | A person | `id68`, `pn`, `birth_year`, `sex` |
| `parent_links` | A child and one parent | child and parent `id68` and `pn`, `parent_type` |
| `individual_years` | A person in a survey year | `id68`, `pn`, `year`, `interview_number`, `sequence_number` |
| `family_years` | A family in a survey year | `year`, `interview_number`, `family_income` |

Three features borrowed from the [PSID's documentation](https://psidonline.isr.umich.edu/Guide/FAQ.aspx) shape the query. First, the 1968 family ID (`id68`) and person number (`pn`) identify a person only together, so every join uses both. Second, `parent_links` has one row per parent, like the PSID's [parent map](https://simba.isr.umich.edu/FIMS/default.aspx), so a child with a mother and a father appears twice. Third, this analysis uses family income, recorded once for each family and year. A family's interview number is valid for one survey year only, so a person's income comes from finding that year's interview number in `individual_years`, then the matching row in `family_years`. I keep years in which the person was the reference person or spouse (sequence number 1 or 2).

Parents and children reach the same age in different calendar years, so I measure parental income by the child's age: the years when the child was 15 to 19. The query also summarizes each person's income before joining the generations; joining two five-year histories first would produce 25 combinations per pair.

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| results: asis
show_code("sql/match.sql", "sql")
```

The query works in four steps.

1. **Find each parent's family in each year.** The first `WITH` block starts from `parent_links` and uses `JOIN` to attach the parent's rows in `individual_years`, matching both parts of the ID. A second join attaches that year's income from `family_years`, matching `year` and `interview_number`. `SELECT` keeps only the columns later steps need.
2. **Line the generations up by the child's age.** `y.year - c.birth_year` turns each survey year into the child's age, and `WHERE ... BETWEEN :p_start AND :p_end` keeps the chosen ages. Names beginning with a colon are placeholders that Python fills in.
3. **Remove the duplicate from two parents, then average.** A mother and father in the same family both find the same family-year, so `SELECT DISTINCT` keeps one copy. `GROUP BY` gathers each child's years, `AVG(family_income)` aggregates them into one number, and `HAVING` requires exactly one family for every requested year. Without `DISTINCT`, the average would look fine, but each two-parent child would have ten rows instead of five, and the completeness check would silently drop `r n(s$two_parent_children)` of the `r n(s$children)` children.
4. **Repeat for the child, then join.** The `child_income` block applies the same logic to the child's own adult family. The final `SELECT` joins the two summaries on the child's `id68` and `pn`, giving one row per child.

With parental income over the child's ages 15 to 19 and the child's over ages 40 to 44, the first rows look like this, in constant dollars. The first two children were born in the same year, so they share a parental average; their sister, born five years later, is matched to different years.

```{r}
#| echo: false
pairs <- read.csv("results/tables/example-pairs.csv")
pairs$pn <- sprintf("%03d", pairs$pn)
pairs$parent_income <- paste0("$", n(round(pairs$parent_income)))
pairs$child_income <- paste0("$", n(round(pairs$child_income)))
knitr::kable(
  pairs,
  col.names = c("1968 ID", "Person number", "Parent income", "Child income"),
  align = "rrrr"
)
```

A Python helper sends the age limits to this query and returns a pandas table, so one query serves every comparison.

## Estimate persistence, then change the measurement window

How closely do the generations' incomes move together? The intergenerational elasticity, or IGE, measures that connection. With the model's IGE of `r f(s$true_ige)`, 10% higher parental income is associated with about `r sprintf("%.0f", 100 * (1.10^s$true_ige - 1))`% higher child income. A smaller value suggests less persistence and more mobility. It is an association, not a causal effect.

To estimate it, fit a line to the natural logarithms of the matched incomes. The slope, $\beta$, is the IGE.

$$
\log(\text{child income}) = \alpha + \beta\log(\text{parent income}) + \varepsilon.
$$

SQL averages annual income amounts in constant dollars **before** Python takes logarithms. In the code, `np.ones` supplies the intercept and `np.linalg.lstsq` fits the line. The checks keep each child once and the children identical across comparisons.

<details>
<summary>Show the Python code that estimates and compares the slopes</summary>

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| results: asis
show_code("tutorial.py", "python", "estimate")
```

</details>

Using one year for each generation, the parents' family income when the child was 15 and the child's at 40, gives `r f(s$single)`. Averaging five years for each raises it to `r f(s$averaged)`, closer to the model's `r f(s$true_ige)`. The families did not become less mobile. Better measurement revealed more of the income connection already built into the simulation.

```{r}
#| label: fig-averaging
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "Averaging several years reduces the distortion from temporary income fluctuations in this simulation."
#| fig-alt: "Two bars comparing simulated elasticity estimates from one year and five-year average incomes, with a dashed line at the model value of 0.4."
knitr::include_graphics("results/figures/income-averages.png")
```

Temporary swings in parental income blur its relationship with the child's income, pushing the slope toward zero. Averaging reduces that distortion. Independent swings in child income mainly make estimates less precise. Five years still imperfectly measure lasting income, and chance also affects this simulated sample.

## Averaging cannot fix measuring children too young

But does averaging solve the whole problem? Holding parental income at its five-year average, I change only the child's measurement age. The slope rises from `r f(s$child25)` at 25 to `r f(s$child40)` at 40. Early incomes hide differences that emerge later. Small dips, such as at ages 31 and 36, are sampling noise.

```{r}
#| label: fig-child-age
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "Changing the child's measurement age changes the estimated persistence even with the same parents and families."
#| fig-alt: "Line chart of simulated elasticity by child age, generally rising from age 25 to age 40 and then leveling off, with parental income always averaged over the child's ages 15 to 19."
knitr::include_graphics("results/figures/child-age.png")
```

This illustrates **life-cycle bias**. Children with higher lasting incomes have steeper early income growth in the model. If everyone's income grew by the same percentage, that alone would not change the slope. [Haider and Solon](https://www.nber.org/papers/w11943) explain why current earnings can represent lifetime earnings differently at different ages.

Even averaging the child's ages 25 through 29 gives only `r f(s$young_average)`. More observations still describe an early career. Real data would also need survey weights and rules for missing years and zero incomes.

The main takeaways are:

* Join on the full person ID, and remove duplicate family-years from two-parent links before counting or averaging.
* Average several years to reduce temporary fluctuations that can make mobility look stronger.
* Compare suitable ages too. Averaging early earnings does not make them representative of a whole career.

[Code, model assumptions, and replication instructions](https://github.com/yipin-grena/aeds6400-blog/tree/main/posts/sql-income-mobility).
